# Exact optimization of the convex-root majorant bound

This note characterizes the optimization in Section 5 of
`candidate af89470c3209e9d8`. It also gives an
analytic obstruction on actual compatible convex fibers. It does not
construct a low-mass cap cover or refute OC.

## 1. A finite program for all convex majorants

Let P be a nonempty finite subset of R^n, let q≥1, and let positive
fiber masses be w_z, with r_z=w_z^(1/q). Put

    gamma=gamma_q,  c=1−gamma,  m=2^n.

For a convex function ell on conv(P), positive on P and satisfying
ell(z)≥r_z there, the established cap-cover bound has numerator

    J(ell)=sum_z [w_z−c ell(z)^q]_+.

Only the values at P enter this expression. They admit an exact finite
description. For each z∈P, take the vertices of the representation
polytope

    R_z={lambda≥0: sum_p lambda_p=1, sum_p lambda_p p=z}.

For every such vertex impose

    l_z−sum_p lambda_p l_p≤0.

Collect these finitely many rows in a matrix D; zero rows can be
discarded. Then the feasible value vectors are exactly the polyhedron

    L={l: l≥r, Dl≤0}.                                  (1)

Necessity is Jensen's inequality. For sufficiency define

    ell_l(x)=min{sum_p lambda_p l_p:
                 lambda≥0, sum lambda=1, sum lambda p=x}.

The minimum is attained on a compact polytope. Its epigraph is the
convex hull of the upward vertical rays above the finitely many points
(p,l_p), so ell_l is convex and piecewise affine on conv(P). At z,
the inequalities for the vertices of R_z imply the same inequality
for every representation; the representation concentrated at z gives
the reverse inequality. Thus ell_l(z)=l_z. All l_p are positive, so
ell_l is positive everywhere on conv(P). This also handles deficient
affine dimension of P, using its affine hull throughout.

The polyhedron L is nonempty: any constant at least max r_z belongs
to it. For A⊆P put

    V_A=min_(l∈L) sum_(z∈A) l_z^q.

Then the exact optimized numerator is

    J_* = max_(A⊆P) [sum_(z∈A) w_z−c V_A].             (2)

Indeed the sum of positive parts is the maximum over subsets A of
the corresponding signed sum. The finite maximum over A commutes
with the supremum over l. Each V_A is attained: the projection of L
onto its A coordinates is a closed polyhedron, all these coordinates
are bounded below by positive r_z, and the objective is coercive in
these coordinates. An optimal projected vector has some lift in L.
For A empty the value is zero. Hence (2) is an attained finite
collection of convex minimizations, not an approximation of the
positive-part objective.

## 2. Explicit dual certificates

Write one nonnegative multiplier lambda for each row of D and a
nonnegative vector eta for the constraints l≥r. When q=1,

    V_A=max eta·r,
    eta−D^T lambda=1_A,  eta≥0, lambda≥0.               (3)

For q>1 put p=q/(q−1) and kappa=(q−1)q^(−p). Then

    V_A=max [eta·r−kappa sum_(z∈A) a_z^p],             (4)
    eta−D^T lambda=a,
    eta≥0, lambda≥0, a≥0, a_z=0 for z outside A.

All these dual maxima are attained. Here is a direct verification,
including the absence of a strict-feasibility assumption. At a primal
minimum l*, the gradient of sum_A l_z^q exists because every l*_z>0.
The negative gradient belongs to the cone of the active polyhedral
constraint normals. Otherwise finite-dimensional separation supplies
a direction satisfying all active linearized inequalities and having
strictly negative objective derivative; sufficiently small steps also
respect every inactive inequality, contradicting minimality. Thus
there are eta,lambda≥0 such that

    eta−D^T lambda=q 1_A (l*)^(q−1),
    eta_z(l*_z−r_z)=0,
    lambda_j(Dl*)_j=0.

For q=1 the first equality is the constraint of (3), and its scalar
product with l* gives eta·r=V_A. For q>1 set its right side equal to a.
It is nonnegative and supported on A. The same scalar product gives
eta·r=qV_A, while kappa sum a^p=(q−1)V_A. Thus (4) attains V_A.

Conversely every feasible dual is a lower bound. From Dl≤0 and l≥r,

    eta·r≤eta·l=(a+D^T lambda)·l≤a·l.

For q>1 apply the elementary Young inequality
`a t≤t^q+kappa a^p` for a,t≥0, coordinate by coordinate on A.
For q=1 use a=1_A. This proves weak duality and completes both exact
dual formulas. The only separation used above is the elementary
normal-cone formula for finitely many linear inequalities; in
particular dependent Jensen equalities cause no constraint-
qualification problem.

The geometric restriction that the r_z arise from actual convex
fibers was not needed for (1)–(4). It is satisfied in the following
obstruction.

## 3. An exact three-fiber formula in every continuous dimension

Take n=1, d=q≥1 and 0<a≤b. Choose a q-dimensional convex body K
containing zero in its interior and of volume one. Define

    rho(z)=b−(b−a)|z|,  −1≤z≤1,
    C={ (z,x): −1≤z≤1, x∈rho(z)K }.

This is a compact full-dimensional convex body. To check convexity,
Minkowski interpolation of two homothetic fibers equals the fiber
at their interpolated scale; concavity of rho and 0∈K include this
fiber in the target fiber. The only integer fibers have scales
(a,b,a), and hence masses (a^q,b^q,a^q). Their total mass is

    M=b^q+2a^q.

For this actual profile the optimized majorant numerator is EXACTLY

    J_* = gamma b^q
       + max{ 2[a^q−c b^q]_+,
               gamma a^q+[a^q−c(2b−a)^q]_+ }.          (5)

Proof. Write the three majorant values as (L,C_0,R). Their complete
constraints are

    L,R≥a,  C_0≥b,  L+R≥2C_0.

Decrease C_0 to b, which can only improve the objective. Then decrease
L and/or R, still keeping both at least a, until L+R=2b. This is
possible because b≥a and again cannot decrease the objective. The
middle contribution is gamma b^q. By symmetry assume L≤b, so
L∈[a,b] and R=2b−L. Set t=a c^(−1/q). If R≤t, both outer terms
are active and their sum is

    2a^q−c[L^q+(2b−L)^q].

It is nondecreasing as L increases to b, so its maximum in this
region occurs at the balanced choice L=R=b. If L<t<R, only the
first outer term is active and decreases with L. Whenever this
region is nonempty it begins at L=a, since a<t and R is largest
there. Thus its maximum is achieved at (L,R)=(a,2b−a). If L≥t
both outer terms vanish. Boundary equalities follow by continuity.
These cases prove (5), including q=1 where the first expression
can be constant. Both candidate majorants are actual affine
functions: the constant b, or the line through values a,b,2b−a.

For instance, if a^q≤c b^q, the second positive part in (5) also
vanishes and

    J_*=gamma(b^q+a^q)<gamma(b^q+2a^q)=gamma M.         (6)

Thus the strict failure of the optimized numerator to reach gamma M
occurs in every q≥1 on actual full mixed-dimensional bodies.

## 4. Sharp one-dimensional continuous example and truncation

For q=1, gamma=c=1/2. Formula (5) simplifies to

    J_*=(a+b)/2 + (3a−2b)_+/2
       = (a+b)/2           if a≤2b/3,
         2a−b/2            if a≥2b/3.                 (7)

In this family the ratio to the desired numerator is

    J_*/(gamma M)
      =[(a+b)+(3a−2b)_+]/(b+2a)≥5/7,

with equality exactly when a=2b/3. The ratio decreases up to that
point and increases afterwards, as direct differentiation of the
two linear-fractional expressions shows. It equals one only at
a=b, or in the limiting case a→0 on the other branch.

Choose specifically a=2,b=3 and K=[−1/2,1/2]. The actual three
intervals have widths (2,3,2), total mass 7, and

    J_*=5/2,   J_*/2=5/4,
    gamma M=7/2,   gamma M/2=7/4.                    (8)

A short direct proof checks the positive-part issue independently.
For every convex majorant, C_0≥3 and L,R≥2 with L+R≥6.
The middle positive part is at most 3/2. If both outer terms are
positive their sum is at most `4−(L+R)/2≤1`; if only one is positive
it is at most 1 because its majorant value is at least 2. Thus
J≤5/2, with equality at the constant majorant ell=3. The affine
contact majorants with values (2,3,4) and (4,3,2) also attain the
same value; their zero term is retained correctly.

This body is centrally symmetric. Its true center has mixed depth
exactly 1/2: every closed through-origin halfspace has at least half
the centrally symmetric measure, and the horizontal through-origin
cut has exactly half. At any other point a horizontal cap on its
side has at most half the mass. Consequently (8) is an obstruction
to this lower-bound mechanism, not a low-depth body or an OC
counterexample.

The other previously proved scalar budget constraints do not fill
this particular gap either. With the formal cap budget B=3/2, the
heavy-fiber bound B≥gamma max w is met with equality, every convex-
majorant inequality `2B≥J(ell)` holds, and the implicit budget
inequality is satisfied:

    sum_z [w_z−B]_+ =5/2≤2B=3.

Yet B=3/2<7/4. This is only a feasible relaxation of the necessary
inequalities; no cap cover with this budget is asserted to exist.

## 5. Additional integer dimensions and combination of contact regions

For any n≥1, take the product of the preceding actual three-fiber
body with `[0,1]^(n−1)` in additional INTEGER coordinates. The
positive base set consists of 2^(n−1) copies of the three-point
profile. Restriction of any convex majorant to each copy obeys the
three-point constraints, so its total J is at most 2^(n−1)J_*.
Conversely either optimizing affine majorant in Section 3, made
independent of the new coordinates, attains this value. Thus the
same exact ratio obstruction persists for every n≥1 and q≥1,
on full-dimensional ambient bodies with d=q. No lattice-changing
coordinate transformation is used.

Finally, invoking the majorant inequality for several contact
regions does not by itself remove its repeated budget coefficient.
For any finite list ell_i and nonnegative numbers theta_i, the only
conclusion obtained by adding these inequalities is

    m B sum_i theta_i ≥ sum_i theta_i J(ell_i).

After normalization of the weights, its right side is at most J_*.
The same holds for arbitrary positive averages or taking all such
inequalities simultaneously. Therefore an argument consisting only
of optimizing or positively combining these scalar majorant bounds
cannot recover gamma M in the examples above. In the width-(2,3,2)
example the two natural affine contact sets are {−1,0} and {0,1};
splitting or reassigning their common central fiber supplies no new
relation between their separately chosen Doignon subfamilies.

This does NOT rule out a geometric decomposition theorem proving
that several contact regions share one cap budget. Such a theorem
would have to add a genuine cross-region relation about the actual
cap cover; it is not implied by the finite convex-majorant program,
its exact dual, or pointwise captured-fraction information alone.

The root-majorant formulation is for q≥1. For q=0 the earlier
whole-fiber Doignon argument applies directly; no power 1/q is
introduced. For n=0 the base has one point and the optimized
numerator is exactly gamma_q M, so this obstruction requires at
least one integer coordinate.
